questions.question: What does `git rebase main` do on a feature branch, and when should you avoid it?
options: It merges main into the branch with a merge commit; avoid it on small branches
It replays the branch's commits on top of main, rewriting them; avoid it on branches others have already pulled
It deletes the branch; avoid it always
It squashes all commits; avoid it before a release
questions.explanation: Rebasing gives a linear history but creates new commit hashes. If teammates built on the old commits, their history diverges, so only rebase commits that are yours alone.

questions.question: A bad commit is already on the shared `main` branch. What is the safe way to undo it?
options: `git reset --hard` then force-push
`git revert <commit>`, which creates a new commit undoing it
Delete the repository and push again
Edit the files by hand without committing
questions.explanation: `revert` adds history instead of rewriting it, so nobody else's clone breaks. `reset` plus force-push rewrites shared history.

questions.question: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
options: None
Delivery keeps every change deployable, with a manual release decision; deployment ships every change that passes the pipeline to production automatically
Delivery is for front-end, deployment for back-end
Deployment has no tests
questions.explanation: Both rely on an automated pipeline. The difference is the last step: a human approval (delivery) or none (deployment).

questions.question: You pushed an AWS access key to a public repository. What do you do first?
options: Delete the file in a new commit
Revoke / rotate the key immediately, then clean the history
Make the repository private
Nothing if no one starred the repository
questions.explanation: Public repositories are scanned by bots within minutes, and the key stays in the git history and in forks. Consider it compromised: revoke it first, then check for unexpected usage and clean up. Secrets belong in a secret manager or CI secrets.

questions.question: Why commit a lockfile (`uv.lock`, `poetry.lock`, `package-lock.json`)?
options: It makes installs slower but safer
It pins the exact version of every dependency, including transitive ones, so every machine and CI builds the same environment
It is required to publish on GitHub
It stores your passwords
questions.explanation: Version ranges in `pyproject.toml` can resolve differently from one day to the next. The lockfile makes builds reproducible, and tools like Dependabot update it deliberately.

questions.question: A bug appeared somewhere in the last 200 commits. Which git command finds the culprit efficiently?
options: `git blame`
`git bisect`
`git log --oneline`
`git stash`
questions.explanation: `git bisect` does a binary search: you mark a good and a bad commit, then test the commits it checks out. It finds the culprit in about log2(200) ≈ 8 steps, and can be fully automated with `git bisect run`.

questions.question: Which steps belong in the CI pipeline of a Python service? Select all that apply.
options: Lint and format checks
Unit tests
Building the container image
SSH into the production server to pull the latest code
questions.explanation: CI verifies and packages every change automatically. Manually pulling code on a server is exactly what a CD pipeline replaces, because it is neither reproducible nor traceable.

questions.question: What characterizes trunk-based development?
options: Long-lived feature branches merged at the end of each quarter
Short-lived branches merged into main frequently, with unfinished features hidden behind feature flags
No branches and no code review
One branch per environment
questions.explanation: Small, frequent merges keep conflicts small and main always releasable. It is the usual partner of continuous delivery.

questions.question: Order the steps of a typical pull request workflow.
steps: Create a branch from an up-to-date main
Push the branch and open a pull request
CI runs the checks and a teammate reviews
The pipeline deploys the new version
questions.explanation: The pull request is the quality gate: automated checks and human review happen before main changes, so main stays deployable.

questions.question: Order the steps of updating your feature branch when the rebase hits a conflict.
steps: Git stops on the conflicting commit
Edit the files to resolve the conflict markers
questions.explanation: `--force-with-lease` refuses to overwrite the remote branch if someone else pushed to it in the meantime, unlike a plain `--force`.
